clinicalPearls: Bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia of the zona glomerulosa is the commonest cause of primary aldosteronism, exceeding aldosterone-producing adenoma in frequency.
Adrenal vein sampling is the pivotal test to distinguish surgically curable unilateral disease from bilateral disease before any adrenalectomy.
Bilateral aldosterone excess is managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists rather than surgery.
Screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio in resistant hypertension, hypertension with hypokalaemia, or hypertension with an adrenal incidentaloma; potassium may be normal.
Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia can cause overt or subclinical Cushing's, sometimes via aberrant membrane receptors producing food- or posture-dependent cortisol secretion.
Germline ARMC5 mutations underlie many familial macronodular cases, so relatives should be offered assessment.
Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease in a young patient suggests Carney complex, prompting a search for cardiac myxoma and skin lentigines.
Cross-sectional imaging cannot reliably lateralise aldosterone excess, and apparently normal adrenals do not exclude hyperplasia.
reference.pathophysiology: Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia denotes diffuse or nodular expansion of both adrenal cortices with autonomous hormone secretion. In the aldosterone-producing form (idiopathic hyperaldosteronism) the zona glomerulosa is hyperplastic with dysregulated aldosterone output, producing sodium retention, potassium wasting, suppressed renin and hypertension. In cortisol-producing macronodular disease, aberrant expression of membrane receptors for gastric inhibitory polypeptide, catecholamines, vasopressin or luteinising hormone couples cortisol release to non-ACTH stimuli, and germline ARMC5 mutations promote nodular growth. Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease arises from PRKAR1A defects within Carney complex. These primary adrenal processes must be distinguished from ACTH-driven bilateral hyperplasia of pituitary or ectopic Cushing's and from congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to steroidogenic enzyme deficiency.
additionalInvestigations: aldosterone-to-renin ratio after appropriate adjustment of interfering antihypertensives
confirmatory saline suppression or fludrocortisone suppression testing
low-dose dexamethasone suppression test and late-night salivary cortisol for autonomous cortisol
germline ARMC5 and PRKAR1A genetic testing where indicated
redFlags: severe or resistant hypertension with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular complications
profound hypokalaemia with arrhythmia or weakness
florid hypercortisolism with proximal myopathy, fragility fracture or opportunistic infection
an adrenal nodule with radiological features suspicious for malignancy
reference.prognosis: Bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism is controlled but not cured by mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and cardiovascular risk persists if untreated; macronodular disease causing hypercortisolism improves after unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy, though replacement therapy may then be required.
pitfalls: proceeding to adrenalectomy on CT appearance alone without adrenal vein sampling
excluding primary aldosteronism because serum potassium is normal
inadequate preparation and drug washout before measuring the aldosterone-to-renin ratio
labelling bilateral nodules as non-functioning and missing subclinical Cushing's
misclassifying ACTH-dependent hyperplasia as a primary adrenal disorder
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on the management of primary aldosteronism
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing's syndrome
management: Confirm the subtype and lateralise with adrenal vein sampling before any surgery, since bilateral disease is treated medically
Manage bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone or eplerenone), controlling blood pressure and potassium
Add further antihypertensives and address persistent cardiovascular risk that remains despite mineralocorticoid blockade
Treat cortisol-secreting macronodular disease with unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy, providing glucocorticoid and, where needed, mineralocorticoid replacement afterwards
Monitor electrolytes, blood pressure, renal function and cortisol status during treatment
Offer germline ARMC5 and PRKAR1A genetic testing and family assessment where familial macronodular disease or Carney complex is implicated
Endocrinology-led multidisciplinary care with surgical referral for lateralised or cortisol-secreting disease
